blocks.en: Abstract
blocks.zh: 摘要

blocks.en: Language models typically increase per-token computation through deeper or looped layers and latent reasoning steps, while richer residual connections improve information flow across layers. We instead increase computational capacity: the number of active computational states a model maintains. We introduce the Lattice of Latents, a set of per-layer horizontal latent streams that run recurrently along time, alongside the vertical residual stream that flows through depth. Like hyper-connections, mHC, and attention or value residuals, the Lattice enhances the residual stream, but rather than adding or rerouting residual pathways through depth, it provides companion computational states that persist across tokens. Unlike hybrid Transformer-SSM architectures, whose recurrent states primarily serve as internal memory for sequence mixing, these latents directly condition the vertical stream's attention, KV-cache writes, MLP computation, and decoding. On Transformers trained on 20B FineWeb-Edu tokens, a 406M-parameter Lattice model lowers validation perplexity from 15.41 to 14.40 over a parameter-matched Transformer. These gains extend across architectural variants. The Lattice composes with prior residual-stream enhancements: with hyper-connections and input residuals, it lowers validation perplexity from 15.41 (base Transformer) and 14.22 (Transformer with the same enhancements) to 13.61. On Gated DeltaNet, Mamba-2, Triadic GDN, and GDN-Mamba-2 hybrids, it improves perplexity at every tested native state size, with Lattice-GDN and Lattice-Triadic-GDN variants outperforming pure baselines with 4x larger native states. These results identify persistent per-layer state as a complementary axis for scaling language-model computation.
blocks.zh: 语言模型通常通过更深或回转的地层和潜在的推理步骤来增加每个地层的计算,而更丰富的剩余连接则改善地层间的信息流. 相反,我们增加计算能力:活动计算的数目表明维持一个模型。 我们介绍Lattice of Latents, 一组每层水平潜流, 随时间而来, 与垂直残余流相伴而来, 纵贯深度。 和超接通,mHC,以及注意力或价值残存一样,拉蒂斯能增强残流,而不会通过深度来增加或改变残流的路径,它提供了相伴的计算状态来坚持跨符. 与混合变形器-SSM架构不同的是,其常年状态主要作为序列相混合的内部内存,这些潜伏物直接会给垂直流的注意力附加条件,KV-cache写作,MLP计算,并解码. 在"变形金刚"(Transformers)上训练了20B FineWeb-Edu令牌,一个406M参数的Lattice模型比一个参数相配的变形金刚将验证棱度从15.41降至14.40. 这些收益跨越建筑变体。 Lattice型由先前的残余相流增强而来:有超接通和输入相余,其验证棱度从15.41(基变形器)和14.22(具有相同增强的变形器)降至13.61. 在Gated DeltaNet,Mamba-2,Triadic GDN,和GDN-Mamba-2等混合体上,它提高了每个被测试的本土州规模的复杂度,Lattice-GDN和Lattice-Triadic-GDN等变体在4个较大本土州的纯基线上表现优于纯度. 这些结果将持久的每层状态确定为衡量语言模型计算的补充轴.

blocks.en: 1 Introduction
blocks.zh: 导言

blocks.en:
Language models accept raw text as input, transform it through internal representations,
and predict subsequent text. Like most learned systems, this process relies on some form
of latent computation. But what, precisely, is the latent computation in a large language
model?
blocks.zh:
语言模型接受原始文本作为输入,通过内部表达来转换,
并预测随后的文本。 和大多数学习过的系统一样,这个过程依赖于某种形式
潜在计算。 但确切地说,是什么 潜在的计算在一个大语言
模特儿吗?

blocks.en:
In a standard autoregressive LLM, each token is processed by a stack of
layers along a single residual stream, and this one latent does several jobs at once.
At every layer, it reads from memory through attention queries, writes to memory
through keys and values, updates itself through the MLP, and, at the top, is decoded
into the next token.
The memory it writes to, the KV cache, is an append-only record that stays fixed once
written; the residual stream carries all of the active computation.
Recent work increases the computation performed on this stream:
deeper or looped layers apply more updates per
token Dehghani et al. (2019) ; Geiping et al. (2025) ; Zhu et al. (2026) ,
continuous latent reasoning continues latent processing between
tokens Hao et al. (2024) ; Wu et al. (2026) ; Zeng et al. (2026) ; Shen et al. (2025) ,
and richer residual connections, such as hyper-connections, mHC, and attention or
value residuals, improve how the stream carries information across
depth Zhu et al. (2025) ; Xie et al. (2026) ; Team et al. (2026) ; Zhou et al. (2025) .

We focus instead on increasing computational capacity : the number of active

At each step of computation – layer ℓ \ell , timestep t t – two streams
of active information are available: the vertical latent h t ℓ − 1 h_{t}^{\ell-1} from the
layer below, and the horizontal latent r t ℓ r_{t}^{\ell} , formed by updating the same
layer’s previous state r t − 1 ℓ r_{t-1}^{\ell} .
In our Transformer instantiation, both latents jointly drive the layer’s attention
and MLP computations. The horizontal latent conditions attention queries and
KV-cache writes, modulates the MLP, and, at the topmost Lattice layer, also
contributes to output decoding alongside the final vertical latent.
We design the horizontal update to be
(a) expressive enough to serve as a useful companion to the residual stream,
and (b) compatible with token-parallel, teacher-forced training.

Although the update resembles those in Mamba and hybrid

There, the recurrent state acts as a sequence mixer: an internal memory that replaces
attention or operates alongside it.
Here, attention (or the backbone’s native memory) remains the sequence mixer, and the
horizontal latent acts as a companion to the residual stream , conditioning
how the vertical stream reads and writes that memory and how its MLP processes it.

In this base update, r t − 1 ℓ → r t ℓ r_{t-1}^{\ell}\to r_{t}^{\ell} , the horizontal latent
receives new information only through the incoming vertical latent (the residual stream) h t ℓ − 1 h_{t}^{\ell-1} .
We therefore add three enhancements that enrich the horizontal pathway: input injection feeds the token embedding directly into every layer’s update,
so each horizontal latent sees the current token without relying on the vertical
stream to preserve it;
a nonlinear depth-wise readout stream lets each layer’s readout of its
horizontal latent depend on those of the layers below, adding nonlinear
cross-layer computation on top of the per-layer affine recurrences;
and top-to-bottom feedback feeds the top layer’s horizontal latent into the
bottom layer’s update at the next timestep, so the most processed state
of the previous token informs the earliest computation on the current one.
The first two preserve the parallel scan, keeping our main models single-pass
at approximately matched compute. The top-to-bottom feedback does not preserve token parallelism, so we approximate it with a
few token-parallel Jacobi passes ( Wu et al., 2026 ; Zeng et al., 2026 ) , at about 2.6 × 2.6\times the FLOPs for three passes during training; at inference, the same model can instead
be rolled out sequentially at the base FLOPs.

blocks.en:
The Lattice is not specific to softmax attention.
We also instantiate it on Gated DeltaNet, Mamba-2, Triadic GDN, and GDN–Mamba-2
hybrids, where the horizontal latents condition the backbones’ native memory-read,
write, and update operations.
After 10B-token pretraining, at approximately matched parameter counts, the Lattice
improves perplexity at every native state size we test;
Lattice GDN and Lattice Triadic GDN each outperform pure baselines holding 4 × 4\times as many native-state entries.
Downstream gains also hold across GDN, Mamba-2, and GDN–Mamba-2 hybrids:
adding the Lattice improves the nine-task average in nearly every
comparison, spanning five native-state budgets and both zero- and five-shot
settings.
Probing GDN’s recurrent memory reveals a structural correlate of these gains:
at matched native-state sizes, Lattice models exhibit more concentrated state
spectra and greater query alignment with the leading memory direction.
These observations are consistent with more effective use of native memory.

blocks.en: 2 Related Work
blocks.zh: 2 相关工作

blocks.en:
Recent work increases how much computation a language model applies to each token.
Along depth , models add layers or repeatedly apply a shared stack ( Dehghani et al., 2019 ; Geiping et al., 2025 ; Zhu et al., 2026 ) ;
along time , continuous latent reasoning feeds the final hidden state back as the
next input, running additional latent steps before emitting a token ( Hao et al., 2024 ; Shen et al., 2025 ; Zeng et al., 2026 ) , with Jacobi-style refinement recovering token-parallel
training ( Zeng et al., 2026 ; Wu et al., 2026 ) .
Both directions apply more updates to one active stream, and often grow persistent
memory with it: extra layers and loop-specific caches, or latent thoughts held as extra
positions, add KV-cache entries.
The Lattice instead increases computational capacity by maintaining one active latent per
Lattice layer that persists across tokens, without adding per-token KV-cache entries.

blocks.en:
A complementary line of work changes how the residual stream carries information
through depth.
Hyper-connections expand it into parallel streams with learned mixing ( Zhu et al., 2025 ) , which mHC constrains to be doubly stochastic ( Xie et al., 2026 ) ; attention residuals replace the
fixed residual sum with attention over earlier layers’ outputs ( Team et al., 2026 ) ; value residuals reuse first-layer values in
later layers ( Zhou et al., 2025 ) ; and input residuals re-inject the
token embedding before every layer.
These methods widen or reroute per-token computation through depth, but none gives a
layer its own state that persists from one token to the next.
The Lattice adds such states and composes with these enhancements: in our experiments,
adding it lowers perplexity on top of standard, input-residual, and hyper-connected
residual streams (Sec. 3.3 ).

blocks.en:
Our affine horizontal update shares the scan-parallel form of linear recurrent
models such as Mamba ( Gu and Dao, 2024 ; Dao and Gu, 2024 ) , Gated DeltaNet ( Yang et al., 2025 ) , and DeltaProduct ( Siems et al., 2025 ) ,
whose transitions remain linear or affine in the previous state.
In these models, and in hybrids that replace attention with SSM layers at
selected depths ( Lieber et al., 2024 ) or run them
alongside attention heads ( Dong et al., 2024 ) , the recurrent state is a sequence
mixer: it substitutes for or supplements attention as the means of reading the past.
In the Lattice, the horizontal latent is instead a companion to the residual stream:
in Transformers, softmax attention is retained, and the latent conditions attention, its KV-cache writes,
and the MLP.
Because this role is distinct from sequence mixing, the Lattice also complements
recurrent backbones: on GDN, Mamba-2, Triadic GDN, and GDN–Mamba-2 hybrids, it lowers
perplexity at approximately matched parameter counts (Sec. 3.4 ).

blocks.en:
Other work brings recurrence into Transformers without replacing attention. Mozer et al. (2026a) argue that feedforward Transformers push evolving state into ever-deeper layers, exhausting depth, and call for recurrence.
NextLat ( Teoh et al., 2025 ) keeps the architecture unchanged and adds an auxiliary
objective that trains a latent dynamics model to predict the next hidden state,
encouraging recurrent-like belief states; the Lattice instead adds explicit recurrent
states to the architecture.
Several concurrent works add recurrent or multi-stream pathways, typically feeding a
deeper representation from the previous token back into the current token’s computation ( Wang et al., 2026 ; Huang et al., 2026 ; Cai et al., 2026 ; Mozer et al., 2026b ) , or separating
state preparation from next-token prediction into distinct streams ( Monea et al., 2026 ) .
Among these, T 2 MLR ( Cai et al., 2026 ) is closest to
our Jacobi refiner, though its recurrent object is a cached vertical representation
rather than a lattice of layer-wise horizontal states.
These works largely add a single feedback pathway or separate two roles, whereas the
Lattice maintains a persistent latent at every Lattice layer;
Appendix A.1 gives detailed description of concurrent works.

blocks.en:
We propose the Lattice of Latents , an augmentation that distributes
computation across a lattice of latents rather than relying only on the usual
single residual-stream latent per token. The latent computation spans two axes.
Along the vertical axis (network depth), the per-token latent is initialized
from the current token embedding and flows bottom-to-top through the backbone’s
layers, where it is updated by attention or recurrent state computations followed
by a position-wise MLP, before being decoded into the next-token distribution.
Along the horizontal axis (time), the Lattice of Latents adds one persistent
latent vector at each layer of an intermediate Lattice block, evolving across
timesteps rather than through depth. Each horizontal latent remains at its own
layer and abstraction level, assisting the vertical stream by conditioning that
layer’s memory reads and updates. In our Transformer instantiation, we additionally
study MLP modulation.
The Lattice thereby increases computational capacity –– the
number of active computational states a model maintains by adding companion
states to the residual stream, which condition the computation of the residual stream, rather than simply widening the residual stream or adding residual pathways through depth.

blocks.en: 3.3 Composing with Residual-Stream Enhancements
blocks.zh: 3.3 与残余结构增强相结合

blocks.en:
Because the Lattice conditions each block’s computation rather than the residual
pathway itself, it combines with residual-stream enhancements without changing the
horizontal update.
An input residual re-injects the normalized token embedding before every
layer, h t ℓ − 1 ← λ r ℓ ​ h t ℓ − 1 + λ 0 ℓ ​ Norm ​ ( h t 0 ) h_{t}^{\ell-1}\leftarrow\lambda_{r}^{\ell}h_{t}^{\ell-1}+\lambda_{0}^{\ell}\,\mathrm{Norm}(h_{t}^{0}) , with learned per-layer scalars; the horizontal update then reads
this re-injected layer input as h t ℓ − 1 h_{t}^{\ell-1} .
This differs from input injection ( inj ), which feeds the embedding into the
horizontal update rather than into the residual stream.
Hyper-connections ( Zhu et al., 2025 ) expand the residual stream into n n parallel streams that a learned router mixes into each block’s input and remixes
after its output (mHC ( Xie et al., 2026 ) constrains this mixing to be doubly stochastic).
With hyper-connections, each Lattice layer’s horizontal update reads the mixed block
input in place of h t ℓ − 1 h_{t}^{\ell-1} , FiLM conditions that block’s QKV and MLP
computations as in Sec. 3.2.1 , and the router writes the block
outputs back to the streams.
A single horizontal latent per Lattice layer is shared across the n n streams.
A value residual ( Zhou et al., 2025 ) mixes each layer’s attention values
with those of the first layer; in Lattice layers, the mix is applied after FiLM
conditioning and before attention.
In our experiments, we compare the Lattice against these residual-stream enhancements
and evaluate their combinations.

blocks.en: 3.4 Lattice of Latents on Recurrent Backbones
blocks.zh: 3.4 经常背骨上的Lattice Lattice

blocks.en:
Although the horizontal update uses a Mamba-style recurrence, the Lattice also
complements backbones that already maintain recurrent memory.
We instantiate it on GDN, Mamba-2, Triadic GDN, and GDN--Mamba-2 hybrids.
Unlike a Transformer’s growing KV cache, these backbones keep native memories of
fixed size: matrix-valued states per head in GDN and Mamba-2, and a
three-dimensional state per head in Triadic GDN, which adds a routing axis.
The Lattice leaves these memories intact and adds a separate horizontal latent that
conditions how they are used. 1 1 1 We use “state” and “memory”
interchangeably for the backbones’ native recurrent memories, which play a role
analogous to the KV cache. The horizontal latent is also recurrent state, but its
role is to condition the computations driven by the vertical residual stream.

blocks.en:
To separate this from simply enlarging native memory, we compare models with and
without the Lattice across native-state budgets at approximately matched
parameters.
In GDN, for example, a 256-dimensional horizontal latent combined with 65,536
native state entries per layer achieves lower perplexity than a pure GDN with
262,144 entries.
We also analyze GDN’s state geometry (spectra, effective and stable rank, and query
alignment with the leading memory direction) with and without the Lattice.
The distinction is functional: the horizontal latent is itself persistent state,
but rather than expanding the backbone’s associative memory, it provides a learned,
history-dependent pathway that conditions the vertical stream’s computation.
We hypothesize that this added computational capacity helps the model use its
native memory more effectively, complementing rather than replicating increases in
memory capacity; our experiments are consistent with this hypothesis.

blocks.en: 4.2 Composing with Residual-Stream Enhancements

blocks.en:
The Lattice adds a horizontal pathway that carries latents across time,
whereas recent residual-stream enhancements reshape how information flows vertically,
across depth.
We test whether the two are complementary by pretraining 400M models on 20B FineWeb-Edu
tokens with hyper-connections (HC) ( Zhu et al., 2025 ) , manifold-constrained
hyper-connections (mHC) ( Xie et al., 2026 ) , value
residuals ( Zhou et al., 2025 ) , and nanochat-style input residuals
(x0) ( Karpathy, 2025 ) , alone and in combination, with and without the Lattice
(Fig. 3 ); the Lattice models narrow the vertical width from 1024 1024 to 932 932 to remain iso-parameter (details in Appendix Sec. A.4.2 ).
On its own, the Lattice lowers FineWeb-Edu perplexity from 15.41 15.41 to 14.47 14.47 , more than HC
( 15.28 15.28 ), mHC ( 14.93 14.93 ), or value residuals ( 14.69 14.69 ), and is second only to x0 ( 14.34 14.34 ).
More importantly, its gains add to theirs: the Lattice lowers HC from 15.28 15.28 to 14.21 14.21 ( − 7.0 % -7.0\% ) and HC + x0 from 14.22 14.22 to 13.61 13.61 ( − 4.3 % -4.3\% ). Lattice + HC + x0 is the best model overall, 11.7 % 11.7\% below the plain Transformer and 3.9 % 3.9\% below the strongest Transformer composition (x0 + value, 14.16 14.16 ). Thus, horizontal latents are not a substitute for a better residual stream; they are an
orthogonal axis that compounds with it.

5 Conclusion
blocks.zh: 5 结论

blocks.en:
We introduced the Lattice of Latents , which distributes computational
capacity across the vertical residual stream and persistent, layer-wise
horizontal latents.
Rather than replacing sequence memory, these latents act as companion
computational states that steer the backbone’s computation.
We use an affine horizontal update and introduce enhancements that increase
latent expressivity while preserving token-parallel teacher-forced computation
within each pass.
LLLMs improve language modeling and downstream task averages across Transformer
and recurrent backbones.
The Lattice also composes with residual-stream enhancements:
combined with hyper-connections and input residuals, it outperforms every
Transformer variant we test.
On recurrent backbones, gains arise at matched native-state sizes and
approximately matched parameter counts,
with Lattice GDN and Lattice Triadic GDN outperforming
pure baselines that use 4 × 4\times as many native-state entries.
Overall, our results suggest that distributing active computational capacity
across interacting latents is a promising complement to scaling width,
depth, memory, or the residual stream alone.

inspires our optional Jacobi refiner (App. A.2.3 ).

Beyond Mamba-2’s gated recurrence, Gated DeltaNet adds delta-rule state updates, and DeltaProduct
composes several Householder-style corrections into a more expressive but still linear
transition ( Yang et al., 2025 ; Siems et al., 2025 ) .
Work on nonlinear recurrences is complementary: ParaRNN parallelizes general nonlinear
recurrences with Newton

We keep the temporal update affine, add expressivity through its inputs and readouts,
and obtain nonlinear feedback across time only through optional Jacobi refinement.
Advances in parallelizable nonlinear recurrences could further strengthen the
horizontal latent as a temporal companion to the residual stream.

Full-Bandwidth Transformer ( Wang et al., 2026 ) feeds the previous
token’s top-layer state back alongside the next embedding; Latent Recurrent Transformer ( Huang et al., 2026 ) reuses a selected high-level
representation as recurrent memory; and T 2 MLR ( Cai et al., 2026 ) routes a deeper representation from
the previous token into an earlier layer through a gated pathway.
T 2 MLR is the closest to our Jacobi refiner, but its recurrent object is a
cached vertical representation, whereas our Jacobi refiner links the top and bottom of a
lattice of horizontal states that each follow their own temporal recurrence.
Recirculation ( Mozer et al., 2026b ) also sends deep activations to shallower
layers across steps, but is a training-free, inference-time intervention with
sequential prefill, whereas the Lattice is trained end to end in a token-parallel fashion. The State-Prediction Separation Transformer ( Monea et al., 2026 ) shares our view that a single
representation can be burdened by multiple roles, but separates them within each token’s computation rather than keeping a persistent latent at each layer.

blocks.en: Figure 9: Ablating top-to-bottom residual-stream flow. Feeding each token’s top-layer state back into the bottom of the network at the next token adds a nonlinear path through the residual stream. Jacobi on vertical applies this feedback to the vertical residual stream, analogous to the concurrent Full-Bandwidth Transformer ( Wang et al., 2026 ) ; Jacobi on Lattice applies it to the horizontal latents; the last bar applies both. We call it “Jacobi” because the feedback is trained and evaluated with three parallel, teacher-forced Jacobi sweeps (J3; App. A.2.3 ), at the cost of extra forward passes. Both forms of feedback help, and they compound: 16.94 16.94 (Transformer) and 15.52 15.52 (single-pass Lattice) fall to 14.92 14.92 with feedback on both. The input-injection and vstream pathways use only information available at the
current timestep, so the base update keeps an exact parallel scan across time.
Neither feeds a higher layer’s horizontal latent back to a lower layer at the
next timestep. Such top-to-bottom feedback is straightforward in a token-by-token rollout,
but breaks the single bottom-to-top sweep of teacher-forced training, because the top
layer’s latent is not yet available when the bottom layer updates. Following Zeng et al. (2026) ; Wu et al. (2026) , we approximate it during training with Jacobi iteration. Unlike
these works, which iterate over a recurrence that feeds the final vertical latent
back as the next input, we apply it to the horizontal latents.

blocks.en:
Building on the 20B-token results in Table 1 ,
Table 3 shows that the benefits of the
Lattice persist under substantially longer, post-Chinchilla
pretraining on 30B tokens. At the matched 400M scale, LLLM ( 908,256 ) (908,256) with input-injection + vstream outperforms Base-24L on every reported
metric, reducing FineWeb-Edu, Pile, LAMBADA-OpenAI, and
LAMBADA-Standard perplexity by 5.4 % 5.4\% , 8.9 % 8.9\% , 8.1 % 8.1\% , and 11.2 % 11.2\% , respectively, while improving the two LAMBADA accuracies by 2.90 2.90 and 3.40 3.40 points. The gains also hold at 600M parameters:
LLLM ( 1024 , 1024 ) (1024,1024) improves over the similarly sized Base-40L by 4.4 % 4.4\% on FineWeb-Edu, 4.6 % 4.6\% on LAMBADA-OpenAI, and 7.3 % 7.3\% on
LAMBADA-Standard, while increasing their accuracies by 1.79 1.79 and 0.75 0.75 points; Base-40L remains modestly better on Pile. Thus, the
advantages observed at 20B tokens do not disappear with extended
pretraining. Moreover, the strong results obtained with different
vertical–horizontal allocations suggest that this capacity split is an
important tuning axis, and that a more systematic search may yield
further improvements.

HC ( Zhu et al., 2025 ) and mHC ( Xie et al., 2026 ) use n = 4 n{=}4 residual streams, each initialized with a copy of the token embedding and summed before the
final RMSNorm.
Each attention and MLP sub-layer has its own router with three sets of weights: read weights that mix the n n streams into the sub-layer input, write weights
that distribute the sub-layer output back to the streams, and an n × n n\times n mixing matrix that recombines the streams.
In HC, following the dynamic formulation of Zhu et al. (2025) (App. J), each
weight is a static term plus a token-dependent term computed from the LayerNorm-normalized
streams. The static terms are initialized so that each sub-layer reads from one stream and
the mixing matrix is the identity; the token-dependent terms are zero-initialized and scaled
by learnable gates initialized to 0.01 0.01 . The attention and MLP output projections are
scaled by 1 / n = 0.5 1/\sqrt{n}=0.5 at initialization.
In mHC, following Xie et al. (2026) (Eqs. 7–9), a single
linear map of the RMS-normalized, flattened streams produces all three: read weights σ ⁡ ( ⋅ ) \sigma(\cdot) , write weights 2 ​ σ ​ ( ⋅ ) 2\sigma(\cdot) , and mixing logits, which 20 20 Sinkhorn–Knopp iterations project toward a doubly stochastic matrix. The static biases are
zero for the read and write weights and the identity for the mixing logits.
In both, the static router weights are excluded from weight decay.
